fields.description_1:
Leeuwbeveiliging serves organisations that may need different kinds of security support, from guarding a location to managing people at an event. A visitor often starts with a situation rather than the name of a service, so a flat list of security terms would make the first choice harder.

The website needed to explain where risk management, crowd management and tailored security planning fit without using fear-based language or broad promises about safety. Trust matters in this sector, but the case study cannot replace proof with words such as expert or guaranteed. The challenge was to make a serious service offer clear, practical and easy to scan, while keeping enquiry routes visible for businesses that need to discuss a specific location, event or operational risk.
fields.description_2:
I organised Leeuwbeveiliging around the situations clients are likely to recognise first, then connected those needs to the relevant security service. Service pages explain the role of guarding, risk planning and crowd management without forcing every visitor through the full company story.

Credibility information supports the choice, while enquiry actions sit near the point where a client has enough context to describe the assignment. The wording stays calm and specific instead of promising outcomes that depend on the real location, event or risk assessment. On mobile, service choices, supporting details and contact actions keep a simple order. The portfolio entry now shows how the WordPress structure helps organisations move from a security question to a useful conversation without repeating a generic service-site formula.

fields.description_1:
Doctorcura combines online treatment information with a medical review process, which means the website cannot behave like a normal product shop. A patient needs to understand the treatment route, answer medical questions and know that a clinician may need to review information before any prescription or delivery step follows.

If those stages are presented as ordinary ecommerce choices, the process can become misleading. The case study therefore needs to distinguish information, eligibility questions, clinical review and practical follow-up without making claims about diagnosis, safety or treatment results. Privacy-sensitive forms also need a calm and understandable path on smaller screens. The central problem was to explain a regulated telemedicine journey clearly for patients to know what happens next, while keeping the portfolio wording factual and cautious.
fields.description_2:
I structured Doctorcura around the medical journey rather than around a simple buy-now path. Treatment information gives context first, followed by the questionnaire and review steps that belong to the service. Practical information about prescription handling and delivery appears after the relevant medical stage, so the sequence does not suggest that treatment is automatically approved.

I kept labels direct and avoided promotional health claims, because suitability and outcomes depend on clinical assessment rather than website wording. Questions and safeguards stay close to the part of the process they explain, and mobile layouts keep forms and next steps easy to follow. The portfolio case now describes the real WordPress flow as a review-led care process, not as an ordinary webshop or a promise of medical results.

fields.description_1:
Koelcellenbouw works on controlled-temperature spaces where the right solution depends on the use, temperature range, size and technical requirements of the project. A company looking for a cold room has a different starting point from one planning a freezer room or cleanroom, so one broad service page would hide important distinctions.

Visitors need enough technical context to recognise the relevant route before they request advice or a quotation, without being overwhelmed by specifications too early. The portfolio copy also has to avoid implying that every project follows the same design or installation process. The challenge was to present custom cold rooms, freezer rooms, cleanrooms and turnkey work as related but distinct services, while keeping technical information and quotation steps clear on desktop and mobile.
fields.description_2:
I separated the Koelcellenbouw WordPress site into clear project routes for cold rooms, freezer rooms, cleanrooms and broader turnkey work. Each route can explain the type of space, relevant considerations and project context before asking a visitor to request a quotation.

Technical details are placed where they help someone judge fit, instead of filling the first screen with specifications that may not apply to every project. Project examples support the service story without being used as proof that a future installation will have the same result. Calls to action remain visible after the key information, and mobile layouts preserve the same service hierarchy. The portfolio case now reflects a custom technical-build process and the decisions behind it, rather than using generic construction or engineering language.

fields.description_1:
Astenadvies needs to speak to people who may know they need financial guidance but do not yet know which type of advice fits their situation. Questions about planning, finances or business decisions can overlap, and specialist terms can make that first step more difficult.

The website therefore needed a clear way to separate service areas, explain what each conversation is about and show how someone can make contact. Because financial content can sound more certain than evidence allows, the portfolio story also has to avoid promises about savings, returns or outcomes. The challenge was to make the advisory offer understandable in plain language, keep trust information supportive and keep the path to a personal conversation visible without turning the site into generic finance marketing.
fields.description_2:
For Astenadvies, I organised the WordPress content around recognizable financial questions instead of leading with specialist terminology. Separate service areas give visitors a place to start, while short explanations show what kind of advice belongs in each route.

Trust information supports those choices but does not replace the service description. Contact actions appear after enough context, making the next step a conversation rather than an implied financial result. I kept the wording measured and avoided claims about returns, savings or guaranteed outcomes without separate evidence. On mobile, service cards and contact routes stay easy to scan. The portfolio entry explains how the site reduces uncertainty around choosing advice, using a structure specific to Astenadvies rather than a reusable finance template.

fields.description_1:
Zeninspec presents technical inspection, testing and certification-related services to decision makers who may arrive with a specific question. Laboratory work, cargo and marine services, accreditation information and certification topics are connected, but they are not interchangeable.

If every service receives the same visual weight, visitors have to understand the company structure before finding the right technical route. The website also needs to show proof without turning accreditation or certification language into unsupported claims about every assignment. The portfolio text therefore had to focus on navigation, evidence and service fit. The challenge was to create a clear hierarchy for technical buyers, keep detail available after the first choice and make quotation or contact routes easy to reach without flattening Zeninspec into a generic inspection company.
fields.description_2:
I built the Zeninspec WordPress structure so technical service areas can be found separately within one company framework. Laboratory, cargo, marine and certification-related routes are separated early, and accreditation information is placed where it supports the relevant decision rather than appearing as a broad marketing badge.

Detailed technical content follows the service choice, which keeps the first steps readable for people who know their problem. Quote and contact actions stay close to the point where a decision maker can describe the inspection or test. On smaller screens, the hierarchy remains clear without hiding technical detail. The portfolio case explains Zeninspec through its real service structure and evidence needs, avoiding generic claims about quality, compliance or performance that are not proven for every assignment.
